To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Muslim population in Uganda is a minority in a Christian-dominated society.

(i) the Muslim population is growing rapidly, and that the growth is not only due to the high birthrate, but also due to the high conversion rate, (ii) the majority of Muslims are Sunni, (iii) there is a high degree of religiosity among Muslims, (iv) the majority of the Muslims are not very well integrated into society, (v) the majority of them have a low level of education, (vi) the majority of Muslim children are educated in private
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which the educational system and educational policies are implicated in the production of the 'good' minority Muslim subject.
the ways that Muslim schools and their students are perceived by Ugandan Muslims, by non-Muslims and by the Ugandan state.
the following questions: How do the Ugandan state's policies and the educational practices of the Islamic schools affect the ways in which Muslim youth understand themselves as Muslims?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Muslims of Uganda are in a state of flux.
the Muslim community in the country is not a homogenous group.
there are no clear and distinct differences between Muslim and Christian education in Uganda, as the differences are only in the names and the way of teaching.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is a work that is a must for anyone interested in the history of the Muslim community in Uganda.
we are working on the issue of how Muslims in Uganda are perceived and how they perceive themselves in the context of a Christian majority.
it has shown how the Muslim community in Uganda is a complex, dynamic, and multifaceted entity that is in the process of redefining itself.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current state of affairs in Uganda is not one of 'Muslim marginality' in the sense of the term as it is commonly understood, i.e., as the condition of being excluded from the mainstream.
the Muslim community in Uganda has been able to maintain its distinct identity and its religious and cultural practices.
Muslims in Uganda are in no position to be complacent.
